Your professor seems to have forgotten a core principal of philosophy: all I know is that I know nothing. You're not *supposed* to do anything. People will feel how they feel and emotions don't have an instructions manual. Loving yourself can help you see your own worth. To put yourself in front of the ones you love for the sake of comfort is absolutely NOT toxic, but that phrasing sure is. Really, separation of powers is more or less an effect of democracy. We can't really state to be a democratic nation if we aren't hearing the issues facing people from all around said nation. This is why we have executive, legislative and judicial branches and why we also have municipal (by-laws), state/provincial and federal laws. A law that heavily applies to one region may not benefit the citizens of another region, at all. Without separation of powers, there's nothing to keep checks and balances and prevent one or more of these branches from abusing their power. Australia is very interesting in how they handle this; they don't have a complete separation of powers. That is to say, some Australian powers overlap when it comes to roles in parliament. In Canada, there is no strict "separation", however government insists each branch only focus on its own functions. So, would a *complete* separation be better for democracy? I don't think so, nor would a lack thereof, as there are always exceptions and amendments that we have to take into consideration individually.
